name: Aviator frames

card.summary: Teardrop-lensed, thin-metal sunglasses frames used to frame the eyes and upper face, long favoured for adding a sharp, structured look.
card.note: Fit matters: frames that sit too wide or too low change the effect.

quick.overview:
Aviator frames are large teardrop-shaped lenses in a thin metal frame with a double bridge. People wear them as a style choice: the shape draws attention to the brow and eye area and the thin metal keeps the face from feeling covered up.

The design dates to 1930s US military pilot eyewear developed with Bausch & Lomb, and the look spread through the military, then through celebrities in the 1950s to the 1980s. Face-shape advice is common in style writing, but no clinical studies exist on aviators and attractiveness.
quick.how: Wearers pick a lens size that matches their face width, a metal finish (gold, silver, gunmetal) and a lens tint. The thin frame and rounded-triangular lens are often paired with angular faces, where the soft teardrop contour is said to balance a strong jaw.
quick.risks: Sunglasses with UV protection also shield the eyes; fashion-only lenses may differ. Frames that sit too low can touch the cheeks, and metal nose pads can leave marks on sensitive skin.

lead: Aviator frames are teardrop-shaped, usually dark-lensed sunglasses with thin metal frames and a double or triple bridge. They were developed so pilots could cover their full field of vision and block glare, and later became a general fashion style. [1]

People use them as an accessory that shapes how the eye area and upper face read: the large lens covers the brow-to-cheek region and the thin metal reads as light compared with thick plastic frames. In looksmaxxing and style discussion they are commonly suggested for angular faces, where the rounded lens contrasts with a defined jaw.
The history is well documented: Colonel John A. Macready worked with Bausch & Lomb on glare-reducing eyewear in the 1930s, and the metal-framed Ray-Ban Aviator went on sale in 1938. [1]

angle.text: Aviators change how the eyes and upper face read in photos and in person. Wearers choose them to balance an angular jaw or to add a classic, military-derived look.

infobox: 1930s (US Army Air Corps with Bausch & Lomb)

paras: Aviators use large, slightly convex lenses intended to cover the wearer's full field of vision. Frames are thin metal, with double or triple bridges and bayonet or cable temples that hook behind the ears. [1]
The teardrop shape was designed for pilots who looked down at instrument panels and influenced later aviator lens shapes. [1]

In 1929 to 1936 Army Air Corps Colonel John A. Macready worked with Bausch & Lomb of Rochester, New York to design anti-glare sunglasses; the 1936 prototype had plastic frames and green lenses and went on sale in 1937. Impact-resistant lenses followed in 1938, and the metal-framed version was sold as the Ray-Ban Aviator. [1]

The Army Air Corps contracted aviator-style glasses in 1935 (the American Optical D-1), and the AN6531 replaced them in November 1941. Photographs of General Douglas MacArthur wearing aviators in the Philippines in 1944 made the style widely recognised. [1]
The style was popular with entertainers and public figures in the 1970s and 1980s, including Michael Jackson, Freddie Mercury, Tom Cruise and Elvis Presley. [1]

Style guides often pair aviators with angular or square faces, reasoning that the curved lens softens hard lines, and some recommend a lens that is not wider than the face. These are style conventions rather than tested findings.

timeline.event: Army Air Corps contracts aviator-style sunglasses (American Optical D-1). [1]
Bausch & Lomb's Anti-Glare goes on sale to the public. [1]
